fieldMarks: Light-coloured body with diamond-shaped spots along the back, outlined in white and black (NDOW).
Alternating black and white bands on the tail (NDOW); band widths are fairly uniform, unlike the Mohave rattlesnake's broad white and narrow black tail bands (NPS Saguaro).
Arrow-shaped head and a rattle at the tail tip (NDOW).
Largest rattlesnake in Nevada and in the western U.S.; total length 30-90 in (76-230 cm) (NDOW; NPS Saguaro).
behavior: Mostly crepuscular and nocturnal in summer but also active by day, especially in cooler months; in the north active mainly April to late September or early October (NatureServe).
May congregate at winter dens; migrates up to 3.5 km between winter den and summer range (NatureServe).
Eats mainly rabbits, squirrels, mice and rats, also lizards and birds; forages actively or ambushes prey (NatureServe).
Often holds its ground rather than retreating when approached (NPS Saguaro).
habitat: Arid and semiarid country from plains to mountains and from sandy flats to rocky uplands, including desert, grassland, shrubland, woodland and open pine forest (NatureServe).
Hibernates in rock crevices or cavities, sometimes in animal burrows; southeastern Arizona populations used creosotebush flats but moved to rocky slopes in winter (NatureServe).
range: Southeastern California, central and southern Arizona, New Mexico, Texas, Oklahoma and Arkansas south into Mexico; in Nevada only the far southern tip (NDOW) and rare in far southeastern California (CDFW). Kansas records may be translocated animals (NatureServe).

lookalikes.name: Mohave rattlesnake
lookalikes.howToTell: Often slightly greenish, with thick white and narrower black tail bands, where the diamondback's tail bands are more uniform in width (NPS Saguaro).
